The Scholarly Work, Torah Teaching and Public Legacy of Adolphe Franck: A Synthesis of French Spiritualism, Legal Liberalism and the Study of Kabbalah
This article surveys the life and thought of Adolphe Franck, a many-sided French-Jewish intellectual of the 19th century who combined a brilliant academic career in philosophy and law with a deep commitment to the leadership of the Jewish community. The text focuses on Franck's pioneering contribution to the study of Kabbalah, which he presented as a lofty metaphysical philosophical system with Zoroastrian roots, a position that changed the negative scholarly attitude toward the esoteric teaching prevalent in his time. Alongside this, the source analyzes his liberal and legal teaching, which stresses the rights of the individual and the role of punishment as a tool of social protection rather than moral revenge. Ultimately, the article stresses Franck's broad historical influence, which went beyond the academic world and also nourished esoteric and occultist currents, thereby establishing his figure as a central bridge between rational modernity and the Jewish spiritual heritage.
The Scholarly Work, Torah Teaching and Public Legacy of Adolphe Franck: A Synthesis of French Spiritualism, Legal Liberalism and the Study of Kabbalah
Adolphe Franck (Adolphe Franck, 1810–1893) is one of the pillars of French-Jewish thought and of academic philosophy in nineteenth-century France [cite: 1, 2]. Franck was born in Liocourt (Liocourt) in the department of Moselle (formerly Lorraine) to a Jewish family of modest means with eight children, in which he grew up alongside his brothers and sisters Adèle, Gabriel who died young, Minette, and the twins Isidore and Jérôme [cite: 3, 4]. In his youth Franck was destined for the rabbinate and was educated by the eminent rabbi Mordechai (Marchand) Ennery, applying himself diligently to the study of the Talmud and of the rich rabbinic literature [cite: 2, 5]. However, because of difficulties in obtaining a scholarship to continue his rabbinic training, he turned temporarily to the study of medicine, and from there went on to the world of general philosophy, in which he found his principal professional calling [cite: 2, 5, 6].
In 1832 Franck achieved an unprecedented historic feat when he became the first French Jew to take first place in the prestigious "agrégation" (agrégation) examinations in philosophy, and in the same year he completed his doctorate [cite: 1, 3, 6]. This success opened the doors of the leading educational institutions in France to him; he taught in Douai, Nancy and Versailles, and was later appointed professor at the Collège Charlemagne in Paris [cite: 5, 6]. Franck enjoyed the full support of the renowned philosopher Victor Cousin (Victor Cousin), who served as his spiritual and academic patron and helped bring about his early election, at the age of only 33, as a member of the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences (Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques) in 1844 [cite: 1, 5, 7, 8]. In 1856 he was appointed professor of natural law and the law of nations at the Collège de France, a chair he held until his retirement in 1887, when he was succeeded by the modern psychologist Théodule Ribot [cite: 1, 3, 5, 9].
Franck did not confine his work to the academic ivory tower, but was deeply involved in the Jewish and general public life of France, which experienced a demographic and intellectual surge following the emancipation of 1791 [cite: 8, 10]. He served as vice-president of the Central Jewish Consistory in Paris [cite: 5, 11, 12], and was a central co-founder of the organization "Kol Yisrael Chaverim" (Alliance Israélite Universelle) in 1860 [cite: 13, 14]. He likewise served as president of the "Society for Jewish Studies" (Société des Études Juives) from 1888 [cite: 1, 5, 7], and served as president of the National League against Atheism, within which he edited the journal "La Paix Sociale" out of a deep commitment to defending the spiritual conception of morality [cite: 5, 6, 15]. His broad social involvement also found expression in his role as rapporteur of a commission of the Institut de France that examined the methods of teaching and educating deaf-mutes in 1861 [cite: 16].
His Torah Teaching and the Study of Kabbalah in the Light of Scholarship
Franck's most famous work, which established his standing in the world of historical research, is "La Kabbale ou la philosophie religieuse des Hébreux" (The Kabbalah, or the Religious Philosophy of the Hebrews), first published in 1843 [cite: 1, 5, 7]. At that time, the prevailing attitude toward Kabbalah among the scholars of the "Science of Judaism" (Wissenschaft des Judentums) in Germany and France was one of contempt and rejection; they tended to see it as a mixture of superstitions and black magic that hindered the integration of the Jews into the modern world [cite: 17]. Franck offered a bold scholarly and theological alternative, presenting Kabbalah as "the heart and soul" of Judaism, and as a lofty philosophical-metaphysical system that arose from an inner drive of Jewish thinkers toward intellectual freedom and independence of thought in the face of the rigid rabbinic establishment [cite: 7].
However, modern scholarship has presented a more complex and critical picture of Franck's working methodology in this book. As emerges from later analyses, Franck's first-hand acquaintance with the Jewish sources of Kabbalah in their original languages (Hebrew and Aramaic) was rather limited [cite: 7]. Franck based most of his knowledge on translations and on the study of Christian Kabbalistic writings and on the research of Christian Hebraists of earlier centuries, such as Baron Knorr von Rosenroth (Knorr von Rosenroth), author of the monumental work Kabbala Denudata [cite: 2, 7]. A comparison of his work with contemporary works shows that it did not carry the same rigorous scientific-philological weight that characterized, for example, the monumental study of the German Franz Joseph Molitor (Franz Joseph Molitor), who delved more extensively into the primary sources [cite: 18].
Franck devoted a large part of his book to the question of the authenticity and dating of the foundational Kabbalistic texts [cite: 17, 19, 20, 21]. He set out to defend the antiquity of Sefer Yetzirah and the Book of the Zohar, developing a comprehensive comparative theory about their sources [cite: 19, 21, 22]. According to him, the fundamental ideas of Kabbalah were shaped during the seventy years of the Babylonian exile, where the Jews absorbed the deep influence of the Persian theology of the Magian faith and of Zoroastrianism, which was then at the height of its flourishing [cite: 19, 22, 23, 24]. Franck explained that the use of the allegorical and symbolic interpretation of Kabbalah ("Kabbalah Symbolica") enabled the leaders of the exile to adopt complex cosmological ideas without creating a head-on collision with the plain meaning of the laws of Moses [cite: 22]. He stressed that Kabbalah is not a mere copy of the Persian religion, for the Kabbalists replaced extreme Persian dualism (the ceaseless struggle between the forces of good and evil) with an absolutely monistic conception that establishes God as the sole cause and the substance of all metaphysical emanation in the universe [cite: 22, 23, 25].
Another central distinction in Franck's Torah teaching concerns the distinction he drew between early and late Kabbalah [cite: 2, 26]. While he admired the Book of the Zohar and saw it as the expression of a healthy and original religious philosophy, he treated the later Kabbalists with utter disdain, especially the Safed school of the sixteenth century, headed by Rabbi Moses Cordovero and Rabbi Isaac Luria (the Ari) [cite: 2, 26]. Franck saw them as commentators lacking flight and originality, who weakened the power of the Zoharic text and added personal fantasies to it [cite: 2, 26]. He went so far as to pathologize the Lurianic system, describing its complex cosmological ideas (such as tzimtzum and the breaking of the vessels) as "the dreams of a sick mind" (aegri somnia vana), expressing a retreat from rational metaphysical thought into a world of hazy images [cite: 2].
His Legal and Political Thought: Individual Rights, Social Self-Defense and the Conception of Nationalism
Franck's legal teaching, as expressed in his principal book "Philosophie du droit pénal" (Philosophy of Criminal Law, 1864), presented a philosophical position that was especially progressive and original for its time [cite: 5, 6]. Franck entirely rejected the principle of retribution and atonement (expiation) as the moral basis of criminal punishment, and rejected the traditional conception according to which the role of the law is "to return evil for evil" or to punish the offender for the sake of moral revenge [cite: 6]. In its place, he set the principle of society's self-defense ("droit de conservation") as the sole legitimate basis for punishment [cite: 6]. According to him, society has an inherent right to defend itself against forces that threaten to destroy its social and moral structure, and this is the sole moral source for depriving the individual of his liberty [cite: 6]. The French philosopher Alfred Fouillée (Alfred Fouillée) praised this theory, noting that it constituted a bold and original breakthrough in comparison with the doctrines of Kant, Cousin, Guizot and the Duc de Broglie, as well as in comparison with the narrow utilitarian and medical approaches of that time [cite: 6].
Franck's political thought was deeply influenced by the liberalism of John Locke, who stressed the value of the individual as master of his own moral and political destiny [cite: 15]. As part of the second generation of the spiritualist philosophers in France, which also included Paul Janet and Jules Simon, Franck tried to balance the principles of individual liberty with the preservation of the moral-religious order [cite: 15]. This conception bore a certain conservative character; Franck and his colleagues held that economic inequality should not be resolved through government coercion or by infringing the right of private property, but that effort should be directed toward moral and voluntary solutions such as charity, compassion and spiritual education [cite: 15]. His aim was to shape a free society in which the individual acts out of inner moral recognition and not out of fear of the authorities [cite: 15].
This complex identity also found clear expression in Franck's attitude to the question of Jewish nationalism and the Land of Israel [cite: 29]. In his late work "Nouvelles Études Orientales" (1896), Franck defined Jerusalem as "an ideal city that exists only in the past and in the future, in memory and in hope" [cite: 29]. This position reflects the worldview of the French men of the emancipation of the time, who saw Judaism as a moral-universal mission and not as a defined political-territorial project [cite: 10, 33]. For Franck, the Return to Zion was not seen as a practical political plan of action (in contrast to the early national movements that arose at that time), but as a spiritual symbol of the aspiration to universal justice and moral perfection that guides the Jewish people in the lands of its dispersion [cite: 29].
Historical Influence: The Passage to Esoteric Philosophy and the Modern Controversy
Franck's historical influence went far beyond the boundaries of the academy and of establishment theology, and reached into the world of Western esotericism of the late nineteenth century [cite: 34, 35]. Although Franck wrote his study from a distinctly rationalist and spiritualist standpoint [cite: 17], his book La Kabbale became a foundational text for the occultist currents in Europe [cite: 7]. Prominent theosophists and esotericists, foremost among them the famous theosophist Helena Blavatsky and the Christian Kabbalist Éliphas Lévi, drew much inspiration from Franck's book [cite: 34, 35, 36, 37]. Blavatsky warmly adopted Franck's thesis about the Persian-Babylonian origin of Kabbalah, and used it to argue that Jewish Kabbalah is a late and corrupted reincarnation of an ancient and far purer "Eastern Kabbalah," belonging to a global primordial tradition [cite: 36].
This process of conceptual appropriation was analyzed in depth in the twentieth century by the renowned scholar of Kabbalah Gershom Scholem [cite: 35]. Scholem, who had reservations about Western occultism and saw it as a distortion of the Jewish sources, pointed to a historical paradox embodied in the concept of "productive misunderstanding" (productive misunderstanding) [cite: 7, 35]. According to him, it was precisely out of the biased interpretations and corrupted readings of Franck's book by esoteric writers that new cultural and creative directions grew, which left an indelible mark on modern thought [cite: 35].
Summary and Conclusions
Adolphe Franck clearly represents the complex attempt of the Jewish intellectual in the French post-emancipation era to hold a dual identity: on the one hand, a patriotic thinker and spiritualist integrated into the academic and legal elite of the Republic [cite: 1, 2, 38], and on the other hand, a fervent defender of the religious and philosophical heritage of his people [cite: 5, 27]. His pioneering study of Kabbalah not only paved the way for establishing the academic discipline of the study of Jewish mysticism, but also opened an unexpected opening for mutual fertilization between the world of rational scholarship and the esoteric revival currents in Europe [cite: 7, 34, 35]. Although his methodology—and especially his reliance on secondary Christian sources—drew sharp criticism from later scholars [cite: 7], his intellectual work remains a fascinating testimony to a formative stage in the shaping of modern Jewish thought [cite: 27, 32].
